passages.t: The empty tomb and the grave cloths
passages.happening:
“Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb and saw that the stone had been removed from the entrance” (verse 1).

She runs to Simon Peter and to the disciple whom Jesus loved: “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb,” she says, “and we do not know where they have put Him!” (verse 2).

The two men run. The other disciple outruns Peter, reaches the tomb first, bends down, and sees the linen cloths lying there, but does not go in (verses 3-5). Peter arrives, goes straight in, and sees the linen cloths, and the cloth that had been around Jesus' head “rolled up, lying separate from the linen cloths” (verses 6-7). Then the other disciple goes in too. “And he saw and believed” (verse 8). John adds that they did not yet understand from the Scripture that Jesus had to rise from the dead (verse 9). They go home (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The first day of the week is our Sunday. The Sabbath was over. Mary comes before dawn, as soon as she can.

All four Gospels make women the first at the tomb, and the note on Mark 16 explains why many historians weigh this: in that world a woman's word counted for little in court, so a story made up to persuade would hardly have begun with women. The note on Matthew 28 sets out the differences between the four Easter accounts, plainly. John tells of Mary Magdalene alone, though her words ‘we do not know’ hint that others were with her.

Notice Mary's first thought. Not ‘He is risen’, but ‘They have taken the Lord’. Grave robbing was a real fear in that world. Nobody in the story expects a resurrection.

The race to the tomb has a touch of humor and a strong ring of memory. Someone remembered who ran faster, who looked in first, and who went in first. And notice the cloths. A thief would hardly unwrap a body and leave the cloths behind, still less roll up the head cloth and lay it apart. Whatever happened, it was not a robbery. Something about what the beloved disciple saw made him believe.

‘They still did not understand from the Scripture’: the disciples did not come to the tomb with a theory to prove. Their understanding came after.
passages.ot:
Which Scripture did they not yet understand? John does not say. The early preaching in Acts pointed especially to a psalm: “nor will You let Your Holy One see decay” (Psalm 16:10). The prophet Hosea had also written, “on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence” (Hosea 6:2), and Isaiah promised that God “will swallow up death forever” (Isaiah 25:8).

John began his book with ‘In the beginning’, the first words of Genesis. Now it is the first day of a new week, early, while it is still dark. In Genesis the first day is the day God made light (Genesis 1:3-5). Many readers think John wants us to see a new creation beginning.
passages.hard:
What did the beloved disciple believe, if they still did not understand the Scripture? Some readers think he believed only Mary's report that the body was gone. But most think John means real faith: from what he saw, the empty tomb and the cloths left in order, he believed that Jesus had risen, before he understood how Scripture had foretold it and before he had seen Jesus. That is why John tells it. The beloved disciple is the first person in the book to believe in the risen Jesus without seeing him, and every later reader is invited to do the same (20:29).

Was the tomb really empty? All four Gospels say so, and the note on Matthew 28 explains that even the story that the disciples stole the body admitted that the tomb was empty. People who doubt the resurrection still have to explain why the first Christians could proclaim it in the same city where the tomb was.
passages.asks: Mary came in the dark, expecting death, and found an empty tomb she did not understand. Ask whether you, too, have come to God expecting nothing. And notice that faith began for the beloved disciple before he understood everything. You do not have to have all the answers before you believe. Sometimes you see enough to trust, and understanding follows.

passages.t: Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus
passages.happening:
Mary stays outside the tomb, weeping. Bending to look in, she sees two angels in white sitting where the body had lain, one at the head and one at the feet (verses 11-12). “Woman, why are you weeping?” they ask. “Because they have taken my Lord away,” she says, “and I do not know where they have put Him” (verse 13).

She turns and sees Jesus standing there, but does not know him (verse 14). He asks, “Woman, why are you weeping?” and “Whom are you seeking?” Thinking he is the gardener, she says, “Sir, if you have carried Him off, tell me where you have put Him, and I will get Him” (verse 15).

Jesus says to her, “Mary.” She turns and says in Hebrew, “Rabboni!” (which means “Teacher”) (verse 16).

“Do not cling to Me,” Jesus says, “for I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go and tell My brothers, ‘I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God.’” (verse 17). Mary goes and tells the disciples, “I have seen the Lord!” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Mary Magdalene is named in all four Gospels. She came from Magdala, a town on the Sea of Galilee. Luke says that seven demons had gone out of her and that she was one of the women who followed Jesus and supported his work (Luke 8:2-3). She stood by the cross (19:25). Now she is the first person to see the risen Jesus.

The Gospels never say that Mary Magdalene was a prostitute. That idea came much later. In a sermon preached in 591, Pope Gregory the Great joined her with Mary of Bethany and with the unnamed ‘sinful woman’ who anointed Jesus' feet in Luke 7, who is not called a prostitute either. In the Western church that picture stuck for centuries, in sermons and in paintings. The Eastern churches kept the women apart. In 2016 the Catholic Church raised Mary Magdalene's day, 22 July, to a feast like those of the apostles, and its decree recalled her old title, ‘apostle of the apostles’, because she was sent to tell them.

Why does she not know Jesus? It is still dark or barely light, her eyes are full of tears, and she is not expecting him. The other Easter stories also tell of people who did not at first recognize the risen Jesus (Luke 24:16). He is the same, and yet changed. She knows him when he says her name. He had said that his sheep know his voice, and “He calls his own sheep by name” (10:3).

‘Rabboni’ is an Aramaic word, ‘my teacher’, a warm form of ‘Rabbi’.

‘Do not cling to Me’: in Greek the command means ‘stop holding on to me’. The old Latin Bible rendered it Noli me tangere, ‘Do not touch me’, and that became the name of many paintings. Jesus is not pushing Mary away. He is telling her that the old way of having him with her is over. He is going to the Father, and something better will come: the Spirit, and a new relationship with God.
passages.ot:
The Song of Songs tells of a woman searching at night for the one she loves: “I sought him, but did not find him” and then, “I held him and would not let go” (Song of Songs 3:1, 3:4). Many readers have heard Mary's search in that song, though John does not quote it.

‘My brothers’ recalls a psalm: “I will proclaim Your name to my brothers; I will praise You in the assembly” (Psalm 22:22). Psalm 22 began with the cry of forsakenness. It ends with praise among the brothers, and the risen Jesus now calls his frightened, failed disciples ‘My brothers’.

And ‘your God will be my God’ was Ruth's vow of belonging (Ruth 1:16). Jesus turns it around: ‘My Father and your Father, My God and your God’.
passages.hard:
Why ‘My Father and your Father’, and not ‘our Father’? Many readers note the care in Jesus' words. He is the eternal Son; the disciples become children of God through him (1:12). So the Father is his Father in one way and theirs in another. But the wonder of the verse is that he is truly theirs now. For the first time in the book Jesus calls the disciples ‘My brothers’. They abandoned him three days before. He calls them family.

Why could Mary not touch Jesus, when a week later he invites Thomas to touch him (20:27)? Readers have answered in different ways. Many think the point is not touching but clinging: Mary is trying to hold on to him as he was, and he sends her out with a message instead. Others connect it with his not yet having ascended. John does not explain further, and these notes do not press one answer.
passages.asks: Jesus found Mary while she was weeping and looking in the wrong place, and he called her by name. Ask whether you believe he knows your name. And notice what he did next: he sent the first witness of the resurrection, a woman whose word many would not trust, to tell the men. Ask whom God might be sending you to with good news, and whose testimony you have been too quick to dismiss.

passages.t: As the Father has sent Me, I am sending you
passages.happening:
That evening the disciples are together behind locked doors, “for fear of the Jews”, and Jesus comes and stands among them. “Peace be with you!” he says (verse 19). He shows them his hands and his side, and “The disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord” (verse 20).

Again he says, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you” (verse 21).

Then he breathes on them and says, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (verse 22). And he says, “If you forgive anyone his sins, they are forgiven; if you withhold forgiveness from anyone, it is withheld” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
‘For fear of the Jews’ here means fear of the same authorities who had had Jesus crucified, as the book page explains. The disciples were Jews themselves. They had good reason to think they would be next.

‘Peace be with you’ was the everyday Jewish greeting, shalom. On Jesus' lips that night it was much more. These were the men who had run away. He does not begin with a rebuke. He begins with peace, and then he shows them the wounds, the proof that it is really he, and the price of that peace.

‘As the Father has sent Me’ gathers up the whole book. John has said again and again that the Father sent the Son. Now the Son sends them, in the same way: in love, to the world, with the truth, at a cost.

Then he breathes on them. The Greek word for ‘breathed on’ is used in the Greek Old Testament when God breathed life into the first man. John may mean that the risen Jesus is making a new humanity. Luke tells of the Spirit coming at Pentecost, fifty days later (Acts 2). Christians have explained the two accounts in more than one way: as a first gift and a fuller one, or as the same gift told by two writers in their own way.
passages.ot:
In Genesis God “breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being” (Genesis 2:7). In Ezekiel's vision of the valley of dry bones, God says, “Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe into these slain, so that they may live” (Ezekiel 37:9). The risen Jesus breathes on his friends, and new life begins.

The forgiveness of sins was at the heart of God's promise in the prophets: “Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity” (Micah 7:18). Now that forgiveness is to be carried to the world by those he sends.
passages.hard:
What did Jesus give in verse 23? This is one of the places where churches read the same words differently. Each view is given here as its own teachers state it. These notes take no side.

The Catholic Church teaches that in these words Christ gave the apostles and their successors, the bishops and priests, the power to forgive and to retain sins in the sacrament of penance, confession. The Council of Trent, in the sixteenth century, made this its main text for that teaching. When a priest says the words of absolution, he does so by Christ's authority, and the sins are truly forgiven.

The Orthodox Church also sees in these verses the beginning of the mystery, or sacrament, of confession. Orthodox teachers often describe the priest as a witness of the penitent's confession to Christ, who prays God's forgiveness over the penitent. God is the one who forgives, through his church.

Lutherans call this ‘the Office of the Keys’. Luther's Small Catechism quotes these very verses. It teaches that Christ gave his church on earth a special authority: to forgive the sins of those who repent, and to withhold forgiveness from those who do not repent, as long as they do not repent. When a pastor declares that forgiveness by Christ's command, Lutherans receive it as God's own word of forgiveness.

Many other Protestants, Reformed, Baptist and others, read the verse as describing the church's proclamation of the gospel. When the church announces forgiveness in Christ's name to those who repent and believe, that forgiveness is real, because God has already promised it. When people refuse the message, their sins remain. They point to Luke's account of the same commission: “repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations” (Luke 24:47). They also note that the Greek verbs can be read ‘they have been forgiven’, as forgiveness already given by God.

All these churches agree on one thing: only God forgives sins, and he has sent his church into the world with that forgiveness.
passages.asks: The first thing the risen Jesus gave his failed friends was peace. The second was a job. Ask whether you have received his peace for what you have done. Then ask whom you have been sent to. If you carry a sin that has never been forgiven, the message of this passage is that forgiveness is real, and that Jesus sent people into the world so that you could hear it. You need not carry it alone.

passages.t: Thomas: My Lord and my God
passages.happening:
Thomas, called Didymus, was not there when Jesus came (verse 24). The others tell him, “We have seen the Lord!” He answers, “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands, and put my finger where the nails have been, and put my hand into His side, I will never believe” (verse 25).

“Eight days later”, the disciples are together again behind locked doors, and Thomas is with them. Jesus comes and stands among them: “Peace be with you” (verse 26). He says to Thomas, “Put your finger here and look at My hands. Reach out your hand and put it into My side. Stop doubting and believe” (verse 27).

Thomas answers, “My Lord and my God!” (verse 28).

Jesus says, “Because you have seen Me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Didymus means ‘twin’ in Greek, as Thomas does in Aramaic. We know nothing of the other twin.

Thomas has spoken twice before in John. When Jesus decided to go back near Jerusalem, where people had tried to stone him, Thomas said, “Let us also go, so that we may die with Him” (11:16). At the supper he said, “we do not know where You are going, so how can we know the way?” (14:5). He is brave, blunt and honest. He does not pretend to understand what he does not.

‘Doubting Thomas’ became a by-word, but John does not tell the story to shame him. Thomas asked for what the others had already been given: to see the wounds (20:20). And Jesus gives it to him, word for word, offering the very thing Thomas had asked for. Jesus does not scold an honest question. He comes back for the one who was missing.

‘My Lord and my God’ is the high point of John's whole book. It began, “the Word was God” (1:1). It ends with a disciple saying it to Jesus' face. For a Jew who prayed each day, ‘the LORD our God, the LORD is One’, these were the words used of the God of Israel. Jesus does not correct him. He accepts the worship.

The Roman historian Suetonius records that the emperor Domitian, who ruled from AD 81 to 96, was called ‘our Lord and God’ in letters sent out in his name. Some scholars think John's first readers would have heard Thomas's words against that claim: the true Lord and God is not the emperor but the risen Jesus. Others doubt that John had Domitian in mind. Either way, Thomas gives Jesus the name no emperor deserved.
passages.ot:
A psalm prays, “Awake and rise to my defense, to my cause, my God and my Lord!” (Psalm 35:23). Israel's prayers called the LORD ‘my God and my Lord’. Thomas gives Jesus the same words.

Israel's confession was, “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Christians have never thought that confessing Jesus as Lord and God breaks that confession. They confess the one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
passages.hard:
Is ‘blessed are those who have not seen’ a rebuke of honest questions? No. Jesus does not send Thomas away for doubting. He comes back for him and gives him what he asked. Thomas's doubt was not refusal; it was a refusal to believe on hearsay something too great to take lightly. Many of the psalms are honest questions brought to God: “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1).

The blessing is a promise, not a scolding. Thomas saw. Nearly every Christian since has not. Jesus speaks to them, to the reader, and says they are not second class. Peter later wrote to such believers, “Though you have not seen Him, you love Him” (1 Peter 1:8). Honest questions are welcome. The blessing is for those who, without seeing, come to trust.

What do Christians confess about Jesus in Thomas's words? The creeds put it into the church's shared words. The Nicene Creed, in the older English wording printed on this site, confesses ‘one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of his Father before all worlds, God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father’. That is what the churches that hold the creeds bind themselves to confess. Thomas said it in four words.
passages.asks: If you have doubts, notice how Jesus treated the doubter. He came back for him, met him where he was, and offered him what he needed. Ask what your honest questions are, and bring them to Jesus, as Thomas did, rather than walking away with them. And ask whether you can say Thomas's words, ‘My Lord and my God’, not as a formula but as your own.

passages.happening:
John steps back from the story and speaks to the reader directly. “Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of His disciples, which are not written in this book” (verse 30).

“But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Many scholars think the book once ended here, and that chapter 21 was added in its final edition. The book page explains this in ‘Two passages, and what the old copies show’. Even so, chapter 21 is in every surviving copy of John that has the ending.

These two verses tell the reader what the whole book is for. John has chosen signs: water into wine, the healing of an official's son, the man at the pool, the feeding of the crowd, the walk on the water, the man born blind, Lazarus, and above all the cross and the empty tomb. He did not tell everything. He told enough.

‘The Christ’ is the Greek form of ‘Messiah’, the anointed king Israel was waiting for. ‘The Son of God’ in John means more than a title for a king. It means the Word who was with God and was God (1:1).
passages.ot: The whole of John's book has been read against the Scriptures of Israel: the Word in the beginning (Genesis 1), the Lamb (Exodus 12), the manna (Exodus 16), the good shepherd (Ezekiel 34), the vine (Isaiah 5). ‘The Christ’ is the anointed king God promised David (2 Samuel 7:12-16), and the one Isaiah saw anointed with the Spirit: “The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me” (Isaiah 61:1). John wrote so that his readers would see that the hope of Israel's Scriptures is Jesus.
passages.hard:
Did John write for people who already believe, or for people who do not yet? There is a small difference among the oldest copies in verse 31. Some read a form of ‘believe’ that means ‘keep on believing’; others read a form that means ‘come to believe’. So scholars discuss whether John wrote to strengthen believers or to bring new readers to faith. The difference should not be pressed. Greek of that time could use either form for both, and the book does both.

Does it matter that John left so much out? Some readers are troubled that the Gospels do not tell everything, or tell it in different ways. John says so openly. He chose, and he tells us why he chose. A witness who says ‘I have not told you everything, but what I have told you is true, and here is why I told it’ is not hiding anything.
passages.asks: John tells you plainly why he wrote: so that you may believe, and by believing have life. Ask what you have made of this book. Not only whether you found it interesting, but whether you believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. And if you already believe, ask whether this reading has deepened that trust, and whether the life John speaks of is the life you are living.
